# Introduction

Standard presentations of the accuracy dominance argument for probabilism, going back to work by James @Joyce1998, show that undominated credences must be _finitely_ additive. Can we generalise them to show that undominated credences must be _countably_ additive? The question has some interest for two reasons. First, a number of questions in formal epistemology turn on whether credences are countably or merely finitely additive. For example, some uses of indifference reasoning are ruled out if credences must be countably additive [@Ross2010]. Second, while finite additivity strikes many people as intuitively plausible, countable additivity is much more contested. This is related to the first reason. Many people think it is reasonable to be certain that one of a countable infinity of states will come about, and regard each of those states as equally likely. In short, there can be a fair lottery over the naturals. That is coherent only if countable additivity is not a constraint.

The obvious way to generalise Joyce's argument to countable additivity would use a measure. The theorist comes up with some inaccuracy measure $\mathcal{I}(c, w)$, meaning the inaccuracy of credal state $c$ in world $w$, and shows that if $c$ is not countably additive, then there is some alternative credal state $c^\prime$ such that $\mathcal{I}(c, w) > \mathcal{I}(c^\prime, w)$ for all $w$. This approach has not been particularly successful.^[This needs filling in. The paper should engage with @Kelley2023, @Kelley2026, @Nielsen2022, @Nielsen2023infinite, @Pruss2022, @KelleyNeth2023 and @ParkJung2023.]

The accuracy dominance argument does not, however, need a numerical accuracy measure. All that's needed is a partial orderings of credal states with respect to accuracy at each world. (Equivalently, a function from worlds to partial orderings.) Instead of looking for a function $\mathcal{I}(c, w)$, we can look for a relation $\succ_{\mathcal{I}, w}$, where $c \succ_{\mathcal{I}, w} c^\prime$ should be read as saying that $c$ is more inaccuracte than $c^\prime$ at $w$. As long as we can (a) justify that $\succ_{\mathcal{I}, w}$ really is an inaccuracy relation, and (b) show that $c \succ_{\mathcal{I}, w} c^\prime$ holds for all $w$, we'll have shown that $c$ is accuracy dominated even if we don't have a numerical measure. That's what I'll make a start on here.

I'll only need to make a start on this project because a sufficient condition for relative accuracy will be enough for the argument. I'll leave it as a question for another day whether this kind of approach could be used to generate a more comprehensive theory of relative accuracy for credences defined over countable domains.

The approach I'm going to develop has three primary motivations. The first is work by Mikayla @Kelley2026 arguing that we should focus on how credence functions compare on finite domains, even if they are defined over infinite domains. I'm also going to take on board wholesale her argument that this kind of considerations shows that credences should be at least finitely additive.

At first one might be tempted to think, indeed I was tempted to think, that this couldn't possibly help with countable additivity. After all, on any finite domain, a finitely additive credence will be equivalent to some countably additive credence, so we can't tell them apart on finite domains. That tempting thought involves a subtle quantifier shift fallacy. If $c$ is merely finitely additive, although on any finite domain there will be some countably additive credence it is equivalent to, it is not true that there is some countably additive credence that it is equivalent to on all finite domains. It's the latter fact that drives the argument here.

The second inspiration is work by Jeremy Goodman and Harvey Lederman [-@GoodmanLederemanArXiV] on axiology for countably infinite worlds. They argue that a sufficient (indeed necessary) condition for $w_1$ to be more valuable than $w_2$ is that no matter how the people in each world are permuted, there is some point $j$ such that for any $k \geqslant j$, the value of the lives of the first $k$ people in $w_1$ is greater than the value of the lives of the first $k$ people in $w_2$. We'll use the same basic idea; it's sufficient for comparative accuracy if no matter how the worlds are permuted, you're more accurate over the domain generated by the first $k$ worlds for all $k$ greater than some $j$.

Finally, I'm borrowing an idea from James Joyce and Brian Weatherson [-@JoyceWeatherson2019]. They argue that when asking which credence function is more accurate over some propositions, the answer is only philosophically significant if those propositions form a algebra. Accuracy measures over non-algebras can have strange properties, and don't seem particularly relevant.

Here's how I put these together. Assume we have worlds $\{w_1, \dots, w_n, \dots\}$. Let $\pi$ be an arbitrary permutation of these worlds, and $\mathcal{I}_D(c, w)$ our preferred accuracy measure over finite domains. (Read this as the measure of the inaccuracy of credence function $c$, at world $w$, over domain $D$.) Write $\mathcal{F}_{\pi,j}$ for the powerset of $\{\pi(w_1), \pi(w_2), \dots\}$, i.e., the algebra whose atoms are $\pi(w_1), \pi(w_2)$, etc. Say that $c$ is **eventually more accurate** than $d$ at $w_i$ if:

$$
\forall \pi \exists k \forall j \geqslant k: \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{F}_{\pi,j}}(c, w_i) < \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{F}_{\pi,j}}(d, w_i)
$$
That is, no matter how we permute the worlds, there is a point after which $c$ is more accurate than $d$, according to $\mathcal{I}$ at $w_i$, on the algebra generated by the permuted versions of the first $j$ worlds. We'll say that $c$ **eventually accuracy dominates** $d$ if that's true no matter which $w_i$ is actual, and $c$ is **eventually accuracy dominated** if there is some credence that eventually accuracy dominates it. Formally, that is

$$
\exists d \forall i \forall \pi \exists k \forall j \geqslant k: \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{F}_{\pi,j}}(d, w_i) < \mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{F}_{\pi,j}}(c, w_i)
$$

The big claim is that if $c$ is eventually accuracy dominated, then it is incoherent. It is leaving accuracy on the table in the same kind of way that violations of finite additivity leave accuracy on the table.

We'll now show that if we measure accuracy by the Brier score, if $A$ is a merely finitely additive credence function, defined over a Boolean algebra with a countable infinity of atoms $\{w_1, \dots, w_n, \dots\}$ there is some countably additive credence function $B$ which accuracy dominates it. The key point is that if $A$ is merely finitely additive, then it is possible to define a countably additive $B$ such that for each atom $w_i, A(\{w_i\}) < B(\{w_i\})$. Since $A$ is merely finitely additive, $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} A(w_i) < 1$. Using this fact, we can note that if for each $i$, we define $B(\{w_i\}) = A(\{w_i\}) + (1-\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} A(w_i))\cdot 2^{-i}$. If we say $B$ is countably additive, then for any $X$, $B(X) = \sum_{w_i \in X}B(\{w_i\})$, so saying what values the atoms take determines the function. Since $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}}B(\{w_i\}) = 1$, then $B$ is coherent, and clearly for each $w_i, A(\{w_i\}) < B(\{w_i\})$.

Now assume we are using the Brier score to measure inaccuracy, so for any finite algebra $\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{I_F(c, w)} = \sum_{X \in \mathcal{F}}(T(X) - c(X))^2$, where $T(X) = 1$ if $w \in X$ and 0 otherwise.





Open Questions

1. Does this generalise to all strictly proper scoring rules?
2. Does the converse result, i.e., that countably additive credences are not dominated, hold when we use the Brier score?
3. Does the converse result hold for all strictly proper scoring rules?
4. Do the permutations play any role in the proof, and if not, what role do they play in the argument?
5. If we bump the Invariably Eventually Better rule from a conditional to a biconditional, we violate truth-directedness. (Proof, it treats all credences that assign 0 to each atom the same.) Is this a reason to not make it a biconditional, or to weaken truth-directedness? (This is related to Kelley's discussion of Zhang.)
6. How does this all relate to the arguments that are raised in the papers in footnote 1.
